Pilled
PILD
verb
The past tense of the old verb to pill, from Old English / Old French peler (Latin pilare, to strip of hair; pellis, skin), “to peel, to strip off the bark or rind.” The same word as modern peel; in the KJV it renders Hebrew pātsal, to peel or strip.

Biblical Definition

To pill is to peel, to strip off the bark or rind—the identical word as peel, only in its older spelling. It belongs to the strange account of Jacob’s husbandry in Laban’s service: Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods (Gen 30:37). He then set the rods which he had pilled before the flocks in the gutters at the watering troughs (Gen 30:38), that the cattle conceiving before the peeled rods should bring forth ringstraked and speckled young—the very sort agreed upon as his wages. The peeling laid bare the white beneath the bark, a device of striped and mottled rods before the mating flocks. Yet the passage must be read to its end, for Jacob himself later confesses that it was no magic in the rods but the God of Bethel who prospered him: God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me (Gen 31:9), and the ringstraked increase came by a dream and a divine hand, not by poplar bark. So the pilled rods stand as a monument to providence working through, and beyond, the schemes of men. Jacob pilled his rods and laid his plans, and God—who needs no rods—kept His covenant, turning even Laban’s fraud to the multiplying of the promised seed.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines PILL as to peel; to strip off the bark, rind, or skin; the older form of the verb now spelled peel.

expand to see more

PILL, v.t. — To peel; to strip off the bark, rind, or outer coat; to lay bare what lies beneath the covering. Jacob... pilled white strakes in them (Gen 30:37).

PILL, v.t. — To strip; to remove the covering of a thing, as bark from a rod or skin from fruit.

PILL, v.t. — Formerly also, to plunder or pillage; to strip a people of their goods (a kindred sense now obsolete).

PILLED, pp. — Peeled; stripped of bark or rind; laid bare, as the white strakes in Jacob’s rods.

PILLING, ppr. — Peeling; stripping off the outer coat or covering; the older spelling of peeling.

Key Scripture

Gen 30:37 — "And Jacob took him rods of green poplar, and of the hazel and chesnut tree; and pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear which was in the rods."

Gen 30:38 — "And he set the rods which he had pilled before the flocks in the gutters in the watering troughs when the flocks came to drink, that they should conceive when they came to drink."

Gen 30:39 — "And the flocks conceived before the rods, and brought forth cattle ringstraked, speckled, and spotted."

Gen 31:10 — "And it came to pass at the time that the cattle conceived, that I lifted up mine eyes, and saw in a dream, and, behold, the rams which leaped upon the cattle were ringstraked, speckled, and grisled."

Modern Corruption

Not a doctrine under dispute but a plain old word for peeling; it recovers the truth that providence, not the schemer’s device, prospers the covenant seed—God keeping His promise even through Jacob’s peeled rods.

expand to see more

The temptation the passage rebukes is the ancient one of trusting the device rather than the God who honours the promise. Jacob pilled his rods and contrived his stratagem, and a superstitious reading has always been tempted to credit the striped poplar with the striped lambs—as if the peeling itself worked the increase. But Jacob himself corrects us: it was a dream from the God of Bethel, and the plain word God hath taken away the cattle of your father, and given them to me. The age loves its own peeled rods—its techniques, its leverage, its clever management of outcomes—and forgets the hand that alone gives the increase. The pilled rods stand as a quiet rebuke to every confidence in method over the Master, in the scheme over the sovereign LORD who prospers whom He will.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is providence overruling the schemes of men to keep covenant. Jacob was a schemer, and his peeled rods were the device of a man still learning to trust; yet God had promised to bless him, and God did bless him—not because the rods availed, but because the covenant held. The ringstraked flocks were the LORD’s gift, given by a dream, wrung even out of Laban’s long fraud. So the believer may lay his plans and use his means, but let him ascribe the increase where Jacob at last ascribed it: to the God of Bethel, who keeps His word to the seed of promise whether the rods be peeled or no.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old English / Old French peler, Latin pilare (to strip) — to peel, strip off bark; the older spelling of peel, rendering Hebrew pātsal in Jacob’s pilled rods.

expand to see more

Latin pilare — to deprive of hair, to strip (from pilus, a hair); and pellis, skin, behind the sense of stripping a surface.

Old French peler — to peel, strip off the skin or rind; passing into English as both pill and, later, peel.

Hebrew pātsal (H6478) — to peel, strip off (Gen 30:37, 38, of Jacob pilling the white strakes in the rods).

Hebrew pātsal — its noun kin petsel, a peeling or strip, marking the laid-bare white of the rod.

English peel — the surviving modern form of the same verb, keeping the exact sense of pilling.

Usage

"Jacob... pilled white strakes in them, and made the white appear—the old spelling of peeled; he stripped the bark to lay bare the white beneath."

"The pilled rods were Jacob’s device, but the ringstraked increase came by a dream from the God of Bethel—providence, not poplar bark, prospered the covenant seed."

"The age trusts its own peeled rods—its techniques and leverage—and forgets the hand that gives the increase; Jacob learned to ascribe the flocks to the LORD."
